newsitem.title: CHINA: China says economy in best shape of '90s, problems persist.
newsitem.headline: China says economy in best shape of '90s, problems persist.

text.p: China's economy is in the best shape so far of the 1990s but faces several striking problems, particularly the blind production of unwanted goods by lumbering state firms unable to adapt to the market, said a new report.
China had successfully guided its economy to a soft landing, said the report by a group of leading economists from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and the State Statistics Bureau.
China's macro-economic situation was at its best since the start of the 1990s, but there was no room for complacency, the report said.

The chief task now facing China's economic tsars was how to coordinate an inefficient state sector with sizzling economic growth that has averaged about 10 percent for the past few years -- without sending the economy skidding off course, it said.

The government could not afford to miss this opportunity to push ahead with new, and yet more difficult, economic reforms -- particularly forcing the state sector to be more efficient in the marketplace, it said.

"Without the launch in 1994 of comprehensive reforms of the tax system, finance and banking and foreign trade and foreign exchange, it would be extremely difficult to attain the rather improved economic situation of today," the report said.

It cited an urgent need to tackle reform of imbalances between supply and demand that have been blamed for mounting stockpiles -- and losses -- at inefficient state factories unable to adapt to the marketplace.
"In 1997, the macro-economic situation is rather good and we should grasp this advantageous opportunity...to make reform of state enterprise the focal point of reform," it said.
The State Statistical Bureau has repeatedly blamed the state sector for growing stockpiles that have hampered growth.
The problems in China's economy were no longer a lack of supply but a failure to raise quality that was resulting in warehouses filled with unwanted goods, the report said.
However, it warned that while tackling the state sector and the issue of supply and demand, the government could not afford to allow the economy to overheat -- or to cool too quickly.
China's economy has been forecast to grow by 10 percent this year, compared with a more cautious government target of eight percent and up slightly from last year's 9.7 percent.
The report urged the government not to cut interest rates again this year after two reductions last year that spurred industry but sent a flood of money streaming into the fledgling stock markets.

"Because of a lack of capital markets that can efficiently absorb funds, there has appeared the current 'overheating' in the stock markets," it said. The Shanghai stock market has gained more than 30 percent since the start of the year.

Industry has been crying out for another cut in interest rates, particularly as retail price inflation was seen cooling to five percent this year from 6.1 percent last year and 14.8 percent in 1995. However, the move has been unpopular among the public, who hold huge amounts of savings in banks.

Beijing should issue more long-term debt to attract the savings of individuals while at the same time providing capital to invest in pillar state industries and thus creating jobs for workers laid off by lumbering state firms struggling to adapt to the market, the report said.
Real reform of the housing market, putting prices within reach of average Chinese and not just the wealthy elite, and tackling the systemic problems of state industry were essential, said the report.
